title: Colossal Archaeological Exhibition of Mesoamerica Amazes in China
author: Emir Olivares Alonso
content:
_This article by Emir Olivares Alonso originally appeared in the[July 20, 2026
edition of La
Jornada](https://www.jornada.com.mx/noticia/2026/07/20/politica/colosal-
muestra-arqueologica-de-mesoamerica-asombra-en-china), Mexico's premier left
wing daily newspaper._

**Shanghai.** It was five lustrums of waiting for China to be able to host
once again a colossal collection of archaeological pieces from the ancient
cultures of Mesoamerica. The Shanghai Museum is the venue for the exhibition
_The Summit of the World 's Trees: Ancient Civilizations of America_, whose
thematic line centers on a dichotomy: that even though they arose thousands of
kilometers apart and despite their marked differences, the worldview of the
American peoples finds some parallels with one of the oldest civilizations on
the planet: the Chinese.

Motivated by the interest in having their people understand other cultures
–which flourished when the first Chinese dynasties were consolidating the
empire–, authorities of the Asian nation worked for months with their
counterparts in Mexico and Peru to bring to this megalopolis **nearly 3,000
archaeological relics from the Olmec, Maya, Teotihuacan, Mexica, and Andean
cultures, of which 804 come from our c** ountry.

It is one of the largest and most complete exhibitions dedicated to the
ancient cultures of the American continent that have been organized not only
in China, but in all of Asia. **The exhibition opened this past day 8 and will
remain open until November 14, 2027. Official reports indicate that so far it
has an average of 10,000 visitors a day.**

> Across 13,000 kilometers, we brought the myths and wonders of ancient

> and witness an extraordinary meeting of civilizations.

Thus, from one of the most emblematic cities of Chinese hypermodernity, space
has been given to understand some of the ancient civilizations of the planet.

Six skulls carved in stone stop the steps of a little girl of about seven
years old in one of the halls of the museum complex, one of the most important
of the Asian giant. Her attitude denotes fear at seeing those objects alluding
to death, but her curiosity dominates her and, little by little, she
approaches. She glances sideways at the Maya pieces for a few seconds and ends
up taking refuge in her mother's lap, clinging to her arm.

The woman tries to explain to her what she is looking at: in the worldview of
the ancient Mesoamerican cultures, death did not represent the end of
existence, but a transformation, the passage to another stage.

The scene is repeated in different halls of the complex: expressions of
surprise, constant questions, and attendees who discover other visions of the
world. What for many Chinese visitors may seem a disturbing image, for the
original peoples of Mexico was part of a profound vision about the balance of
the universe and the cycle of life.

According to the Shanghai Museum, the exhibition constitutes "the largest
exhibition of its kind" organized since 2001, when the venue presented the
exhibition _Maya Treasures from Mexico_ ; in addition to being the most
extensive and complete presentation dedicated to the ancient civilizations of
the American continent carried out to date.

From the beginning of the tour, **the exhibition poses a central idea: the
ancient civilizations of China and America, although separated by an immense
ocean, posed similar questions about the origin of the universe, the passage
of time, the relationship with nature, and the role of the human being within
the cosmos.**

## The Exhibition Represents a Dialogue Between Ancient Cultures

For the director of the Shanghai Museum, Chu Xiaobo, the exhibition represents
a dialogue between ancient cultures.** "Chinese civilization and the Latin
American ones have many points in common in their worldview,"** he told the
Xinhua agency on the day of the inauguration, highlighting that the cultures
of America and China developed calendars, astronomical knowledge, complex
agricultural systems, and a profound symbolic relationship with elements of
nature.

![](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/1mi2u12000t6l3mqi2D80.webp)

One of the greatest symbols of the exhibition is the Colossal Head 4 of San
Lorenzo, of Olmec origin, the so-called mother culture. This civilization
arose, according to historical reports, between 1600 and 1500, when the Shang
dynasty was beginning in China.

The piece, of approximately 4.5 tons and almost 3,000 years old, traveled more
than 13,000 kilometers from Mexico to Shanghai. Its transfer represented a
complex international operation of conservation, packing, security, and
transport that translated into working sessions of Mexican and Chinese
archaeologists, restorers, heritage specialists, and technical teams.

The consul of cultural affairs and cooperation of the consulate of Mexico in
Shanghai, Rodrigo Topete Maza, notes in conversation with this newspaper that
exhibitions like this one –which takes place within the framework of the 55th
anniversary of the establishment of relations between our country and the
People's Republic of China, next year– strengthen mutual knowledge, promote
respect for heritage, and generate new opportunities for cooperation between
museums, universities, researchers, and cultural institutions.

"It is a reminder that the bilateral relationship is not only built through
political dialogue or economic cooperation, but also through cultural exchange
and the recognition of the deep historical roots of both peoples. The
exhibition reflects the growing interest that exists in China in learning
about the cultural heritage of Mexico."

In another hall, visitors discover one of the most surprising spaces of
Teotihuacan: the representation of the tunnel found beneath the temple of
Quetzalcóatl. The feathered serpent, one of the most important figures of
Mesoamerica, appears as a symbol of union between the earth and the sky: the
force of nature and divine power.

> Walk through a recreated tunnel beneath the Feathered Serpent Pyramid and
> enter a world of ancient ritual. As you approach the figures found at its
> end, follow a royal heir on a journey of learning and symbolic rebirth
> before he ascends the throne.
> [#OnTopoftheWorldTree](https://x.com/hashtag/OnTopoftheWorldTree?src=hash&ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)
> [pic.twitter.com/VeVKkM61EA](https://t.co/VeVKkM61EA)
>
> -- Shanghai Museum (@ShanghaiMuseum) [July 14,
> 2026](https://x.com/ShanghaiMuseum/status/2076850991618514946?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)

For many Chinese attendees, the image turns out to be familiar in a symbolic
sense, since they associate it with the dragon. The presence of mythological
beings associated with the sky, the sacred animals, and the connection between
rulers and supernatural forces recall some ideas also present in the tradition
of this country.

The Mexica culture occupies a prominent place in the exhibition. Its temples,
deities, and ritual objects show a society organized around agriculture, war,
and the need to maintain the cosmic balance. A replica of the Sun Stone is
presented, onto which a light show is projected that allows visitors to
understand how the Mexica conceived of time as a cycle. The universe had to be
kept in motion, and human sacrifice was interpreted as a form of renewal and
continuity.

This is one of the parts that most provokes surprise on this side of the
world. Miss Li, a young Chinese woman of 22 years, acknowledges that the
sacrifice rituals were one of the aspects that most caught her attention. "Now
it may seem something difficult to understand. Although it is something not so
nice, in that era it had an indispensable meaning within that society," she
comments.

The Maya presence is another of the great attractions of the exhibition.
Calendars, sculptures, and objects related to rulers make it possible to learn
about a civilization that achieved extraordinary advances in astronomy,
writing, mathematics, and architecture. The replica of the tomb of Pakal,
ruler of Palenque –discovered in 1952–, allows visitors to get close to the
reliefs associated with his journey to the beyond. Some even touch with
amazement the carved representations, trying to understand a history that
occurred more than a thousand years ago.

**The second part of the exhibition takes the visitor toward the Andes.**
There, gold appears not as a symbol of economic wealth, but as a sacred
material related to the gods, power, and the connection with the ancestors.
The Andean cultures used gold, silver, copper, stone, textiles, and ceramics
to represent their beliefs, their social hierarchies, and their interpretation
of the universe.

**The magnitude of the exhibition was possible thanks to the collaboration
between Mexican, Peruvian, and Chinese institutions, in a project that
required more than 18 months of preparation.**

Guo Cunhai, director of the Office of Social and Cultural Research of the
Latin American Institute of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, affirms
that the encounter between both regions makes it possible to build a more
diverse world narrative, in which no civilization represents a single path of
development. **" Civilizations do not develop in a single line," and mutual
learning is important, he emphasized.**

Among gods, calendars, sacred trees, and memories in stone, the cultures of
America make evident a history that could not be eradicated by the long and
violent stage of colonization and survived the passage of time, and in the
coming months it will dialogue with China from the heart of Shanghai.
